explanations: luna: The section explains dīn as judgment, accounting, and requital, then names this verse: God is “Master of the Day of dīn” (مالك يوم الدين), so the day belongs to the One who rules it. | terra: "مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ" names the worshiped Lord as owner of the day of judgment, account, and recompense developed in the section.
terra: After naming God owner of the Day of dīn, the worshipers say that they worship Him alone and seek His aid; the Judge and the worshiped one are contiguous in the prayer's own voice.
terra: God gives life to the dead, causes death, gives life again, and to Him people are returned; the whole return-to-Judge sequence is compressed into one ayah.

luna: After rival scriptural communities dispute, the ayah says God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection; it is a direct instance of the judgment over disagreement named in the section. | terra: Mutually condemning scriptural communities are told that God will judge their dispute on the Day of Resurrection, a direct repeated occurrence of the section's court scene.

terra: People are forbidden to pass wealth to rulers or judges in order to consume others' property sinfully; corrupted judgment produces the injustice that the section's root account says حكم should prevent.
terra: God sends scripture in truth to judge between people concerning their disputes, locating sound adjudication in revealed guidance.
terra: The one God is named "الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ", matching the divine title before whom the section's dictionary account says creation stands on the Resurrection Day.

terra: "No compulsion in dīn" marks a boundary around the root's worldly subjection sense: the Quranic religion in this ayah is entered after truth is distinguished from error, not imposed as enslavement.

luna: God asks Abraham “Do you not believe?” and Abraham answers “Yes indeed” (قال بلى); in a discussion of reviving the dead, this is another exact instance of the negative-question answer pattern the section explains. | terra: God asks Abraham "أَوَلَمْ تُؤْمِنْ" and he answers "بَلَىٰ" before the demonstration of reviving birds; the same grammar joins affirmation to confidence in resurrection.

luna: The section's named dictionary branch ḥikma defines wisdom as finding truth through knowledge and reason; this ayah names wisdom (الحكمة) as a gift from God and calls it abundant good, a direct use of that branch. | terra: God gives wisdom to whom He wills, and its recipient has abundant good; the h-k-m derivative names a divinely granted capacity for right discernment.
terra: People are warned of a day when they are returned to God, every soul is paid in full, and none is wronged; return, recompense, and restraint of injustice coincide.
terra: "لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ" joins the sole worshiped God to the Living, Self-Sustaining name used in the section's standing scene.
terra: The Book contains "آيَاتٌ مُحْكَمَاتٌ" that anchor it, while crooked hearts pursue ambiguity; firmness of wording restrains interpretive deviation.
terra: God, the angels, and people of knowledge testify that there is no deity but Him while He upholds justice; sole worship, knowledge, and the maintenance of equity meet in one formulation.
terra: People given scripture are called to God's Book "لِيَحْكُمَ بَيْنَهُمْ", yet a party turns away; this is the section's scene of summoning parties to divine judgment and their refusal.

luna: People are gathered on a day of no doubt and every soul is paid in full for what it earned without injustice; it is a direct expansion of dīn as accounting and requital. | terra: When all are gathered on the doubtless day, every soul is paid fully and none is wronged, directly describing the just decision anticipated by the section.

luna: The prayer names God “Master of sovereignty” and asks Him to give or take dominion, honor or abase whom He wills; this supplies a concrete instance of the ownership and subjection in the section's d-y-n gloss.

luna: God says that the disputants return to Him and that He will judge between them over what they differed about; it puts the section's return and judgment together on the resurrection horizon. | terra: God tells Jesus that all parties return to Him and He will judge their disputes; return and decision are explicitly the endpoint of their division.
terra: A human given scripture, judgment, and prophethood cannot tell people to worship him instead of God; possession of حكم is sharply distinguished from being the one worshiped.

luna: All in the heavens and earth submit to God willingly or unwillingly and return to Him; this makes the section's d-y-n branch of subjection and its return-to-the-Judge motif explicit. | terra: All in heaven and earth submits to God willingly or unwillingly and is returned to Him, giving a nonlexical statement of the source dictionary's dīn sense of subjection.
luna: Every soul tastes death and receives its full recompense on the Day of Resurrection; the verse spells out the accounting and requital the section reads in dīn.
terra: A marital breach calls for an arbiter from each family, and sincere desire for reconciliation receives God's aid; human حكم is explicitly a restraint exercised for إصلاح.
terra: God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies good, supplying a concise measure of the justice attributed to the best Judge.

luna: The section defines ḥukm as restraint from injustice; this command explicitly joins judging among people to justice (أن تحكموا بالعدل), giving that definition a public practice. | terra: God commands trusts to be restored and commands that, when people judge, they judge with justice; this is the section's dictionary sense of restraint from wrongdoing made normative.

luna: The command “refer it back to God and the Messenger” (فردّوه إلى الله والرسول) sends disputes to divine judgment. The ayah's radd is a different root from the section's dictionary form aḥkamtu (“I returned him”), but makes the same movement toward adjudication. | terra: Disputes are to be referred to God and the Messenger, supplying the practical act behind the section's phrase about calling parties to God's judgment.

luna: This ayah exposes people who claim belief but seek judgment from ṭāghūt after being told to reject it; it is a specific opposing recourse to the call to God's judgment in 4:59. | terra: Those claiming belief seek the judgment of ṭāghūt despite being commanded to reject it; the ayah exposes the rival submission implied whenever God's judgment is refused.
terra: When hypocrites are told to come to what God revealed and to the Messenger, they turn away emphatically, continuing 4:60's rejected summons to judgment.

luna: The section describes calling parties to God's ruling; this ayah says faith requires making the Messenger judge their dispute and then submitting without resistance to his decision. | terra: Faith is denied until people make the Messenger judge their disputes, feel no inward resistance, and submit fully; accepting judgment becomes concrete willing subjection.
terra: The one God promises to gather everyone on the doubtless Resurrection Day and asks who is truer in speech; sole deity, gathering, and a question demanding assent coincide.
terra: The Book is sent in truth so the Prophet may judge people by what God has shown him, while he is forbidden to advocate for betrayers; revelation reins in partiality.

terra: God sends the Book and wisdom to the Prophet and teaches him what he did not know in the context of protecting him from a partisan misjudgment; wisdom and revealed knowledge secure the true verdict.

luna: The command to stand for justice even against oneself, parents, and kin checks partiality; it echoes the section's ḥukm as restraint from injustice and its image of holding back what would run unchecked. | terra: Believers must stand firmly for justice even against themselves or close kin and must not follow desire; self-restraint makes truthful judgment possible.
terra: God judges believers and hypocrites on the Day of Resurrection and denies unbelievers a final way over believers, making judgment the definitive settlement.

luna: The ayah warns that hatred must not carry people into injustice and commands justice; this is a specific moral restraint like the section's explanation of ḥukm as holding back wrongdoing. | terra: Hatred must not drive believers away from justice; the command to be just makes restraint from wrongdoing operate precisely when passion pushes hardest.
terra: If the Prophet judges the parties who come to him, he must judge equitably, and God loves the equitable; the ayah states the corrective justice built into the section's root account.
terra: They ask the Prophet to judge although the Torah contains "حُكْمُ اللَّهِ", then turn away; the ayah combines possession of divine judgment with refusal to submit to it.
terra: Prophets judge by the Torah God revealed, and refusal to judge by revelation is named unbelief; transmitted law places a firm boundary on the judge.
terra: The revealed law sets measured redress for injuries and calls those who do not judge by God's revelation wrongdoers, making judgment itself a check on ظلم.
terra: The people of the Gospel are told to judge by what God revealed, and refusal is called defiance; divine judgment is presented as a binding corrective norm.
terra: The Prophet must judge by what God revealed and resist desires; the ayah then makes God the common return who will disclose disputed matters.

luna: The command to judge by what God revealed and not follow people's desires (ولا تتبع أهواءهم) shows judgment restraining partiality; the section's ḥ-k-m image moves from holding back harm to deciding justly. | terra: The command to judge by revelation is coupled with warnings against desires and seduction away from God's rulings, presenting judgment as active restraint for correction.

luna: The section asks whether God is not the wisest of judges; this ayah asks “who is better than God in judgment?” (ومن أحسن من الله حكما), contrasting God's judgment with the judgment of ignorance. | terra: The question "وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ حُكْمًا" is a near counterpart to 95:8, while its contrast with جاهلية makes God's best judgment the boundary against distorted human rule.
terra: Compensation for deliberately hunted game is assessed by two just persons; judgment measures a corrective due rather than giving appetite free rein.
terra: Everyone's return is to God, who then informs them of what they did; return carries directly into disclosure and account.
terra: Standing over the Fire, deniers wish they could be returned and cease denying; the scene reveals too late what the section's present question asks them to affirm now.
terra: God says that, if returned, they would resume what was forbidden; mere reversal to earthly life would not accomplish the corrective restraint imagined by their plea.

luna: When people stand before their Lord, they are asked “Is this not the truth?” and answer yes (قالوا بلى وربنا); this supplies the section's negative-question/affirmative-answer form in a judgment scene. | terra: When people are made to stand before their Lord, He asks "أَلَيْسَ هَذَا بِالْحَقِّ" and they answer "بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّنَا"; the section's question-and-affirmation form occurs inside final judgment.

luna: “Judgment belongs only to God” (إن الحكم إلا لله), who tells the truth and is the best divider, closely matches the section's account of ḥukm as God's just decision. | terra: The Prophet says "إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ" and that God tells the truth and is the best separator, making divine judgment an act that distinguishes truth rather than mere power.

luna: The next ayah after 6:57 says that if what the opponents hasten were with the Prophet, the matter between them would already be decided; it continues the passage's boundary between God's judgment and human demands for it.
terra: God is the subduer over His servants and sends guardians until death's messengers take a soul; this supplies the divine mastery and death scene immediately before 6:62's return and judgment.

luna: This ayah joins the section's two distinct words: the dead are “returned” (رُدّوا) to their true Master, then “judgment” (الحكم) is declared His. The return of 95:5 and rule of 95:8 become one scene. | terra: The dead are "رُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ" and the same ayah declares "لَهُ الْحُكْمُ"; it fuses the section's returning hand, true Master, and final Judge in one scene.
luna: God's word is true and sovereignty is His on the day the trumpet is blown; this joins the section's rule of the Judge to the appointed resurrection scene.
terra: People come to God individually as He created them the first time, leaving bestowed possessions behind; first creation becomes the form of return and dispossession before judgment.

luna: The question “shall I seek another judge besides God?” (أفغير الله أبتغي حكما) names the same divine adjudication that the section finds in al-ḥākimīn. | terra: "أَفَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أَبْتَغِي حَكَمًا" rejects seeking any other judge because God sent the fully explained Book; the rhetorical question places the proper answer in the hearer's mouth.
terra: Arbitrary shares are assigned to God and alleged partners, ending "سَاءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ"; invented cultic judgment reverses the section's union of worship and God's rule.
terra: Good is repaid tenfold while evil receives only its equivalent and none are wronged; recompense is both measured and merciful.
terra: No soul bears another's burden; all return to their Lord, who tells them the truth about their disputes, joining individual responsibility, return, and final clarification.
terra: The weighing on that day is declared true, and heavy scales identify the successful; the Judge's decision is represented as exact measurement.
luna: The command says, “as He originated you, so you will return” (كما بدأكم تعودون); this closely links the section's created human in 95:4 to the return in 95:5.

luna: The section's “khayru l-ḥākimīn” refrain appears as Shuʿayb tells his people to wait until God judges between them; it gives the section's final question a voice of patience amid division. | terra: Shuayb tells the believing and unbelieving parties to wait until God judges between them, calling Him "خَيْرُ الْحَاكِمِينَ"; judgment restrains a conflict people cannot settle.

terra: Shuayb's chiefs threaten expulsion unless the believers return to their community's creed, even unwillingly; coerced worldly return and subjection stand against waiting for God's judgment in 7:87.

luna: After Shuʿayb's people threaten to expel him and the believers, he asks God to “open/judge between us and our people with truth” (افتح بيننا وبين قومنا بالحق); this makes the section's ḥukm a resolution of threatened injustice. | terra: Shuayb prays for God to decide between his people and the believers in truth, calling Him the best opener; a different verb voices the same entrusting of conflict to God.

luna: The messenger is said to remove burdens and shackles from people; this reverses the section's bridle as a restraining instrument and distinguishes correction that holds back wrongdoing from restraints that are themselves lifted.

luna: The negative question “Am I not your Lord?” (ألست بربكم) receives “Yes indeed” (قالوا بلى); the section explains that a question framed with negation expects the confirming answer balā. | terra: The covenant question "أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ" receives "بَلَىٰ"; it is the section's exact grammatical model for a negative question that demands affirmation.

luna: The section's dictionary image is a ring around a horse's jaw that restrains it; this ayah mentions tethered warhorses (رباط الخيل). This is a weak scene parallel because the verse is about military readiness, not a corrective bridle.
terra: Those offering excuses are told they will be returned to the Knower of unseen and seen, who will report their deeds; concealed motives cannot evade the returning Judge.
terra: People are told to act and are then "تُرَدُّونَ" to the Knower of unseen and seen, who informs them of their deeds; return leads directly to disclosure and account.

luna: God begins creation and repeats it, then people return to Him to receive just recompense; this connects the section's creation, return, and dīn as requital. | terra: All return to God; He begins and repeats creation so believers are recompensed in justice, making creation, resurrection, return, and fair judgment one argument.
luna: After people divide, the ayah says God would judge between them on the Day of Resurrection over their disagreement; it is another direct formulation of the section's delayed judgment.

luna: On that day each soul encounters what it did and people are returned to their true Master (وردوا إلى الله مولاهم الحق); this supplies a second scene of return to the owner who judges. | terra: Every soul tests its prior deeds and all are "رُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلَاهُمُ الْحَقِّ"; this closely repeats 6:62's return to the true Master before false supports vanish.
terra: After contrasting God, who guides to truth, with powerless partners, the ayah asks "فَمَا لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ"; accurate judgment must follow the one who reaches and guides to truth.
terra: Every community has a messenger, and when its messenger comes the people are judged equitably without injustice; witness, decision, and the prevention of ظلم form one scene.
terra: When every wrongdoer sees the punishment, judgment is made in equity and no one is wronged, continuing the section's court meaning without the h-k-m root.
terra: After the Children of Israel divide despite knowledge, their Lord will judge their disputes on the Resurrection Day; knowledge without right judgment becomes accountable.

luna: The section names the same “khayru l-ḥākimīn” wording in the command to the Prophet to wait for God's judgment; this makes the final question a ground for patient trust, not only a claim about divine rank. | terra: The Messenger is told to follow revelation and endure "حَتَّىٰ يَحْكُمَ اللَّهُ" because He is the best of judges, directly matching the section's stance of waiting for God's decision.
terra: The Book's verses are "أُحْكِمَتْ" and then detailed by one Wise and Aware; the h-k-m root here means made firm or precise, a distinct extension of restraining disorder.
terra: Noah's son trusts a mountain to save him, but the wave separates them and he is drowned; this is the anguish within which 11:45 names God best Judge.
terra: The flood is commanded to subside and "قُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ"; the settled decree immediately precedes Noah's appeal to the best of judges.

luna: The section's source phrase “aḥkamu l-ḥākimīn” is spoken by Noah while pleading for his son, whom he calls family and ties to God's promise; the plea shows how trust in the best Judge meets a painful family case. | terra: Noah appeals over his drowned son and says "أَنْتَ أَحْكَمُ الْحَاكِمِينَ"; the section's closing title becomes the language of trust when a divine decision is painful.

luna: The section cites Noah's appeal in 11:45 for his son as family; the next ayah answers that the son is not of his family in the relevant sense and warns Noah not to ask without knowledge, showing the limit that divine judgment sets on kinship. | terra: God rules that Noah's son is not of his true family because his conduct is unrighteous and warns Noah against asking without knowledge; divine judgment corrects kinship-based expectation.

luna: After the correction in 11:46, Noah seeks refuge from asking what he does not know and asks for mercy; this next turn shows him accepting the Judge's correction. | terra: Noah seeks refuge and forgiveness after the correction, showing submission to the judgment he had invoked in 11:45.
terra: God holds every creature by its forelock and the Lord is on a straight path; bodily control of the head supplies a close nonlexical analogue to the source dictionary's guiding bridle.
terra: When Joseph matures, God gives him "حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا"; the pairing concretely supports the section's link between judgment, wisdom, and knowledge.

luna: This ayah joins two roots named in the section: “judgment belongs only to God” (إن الحكم إلا لله), and God commands worship of Him alone, “that is the upright dīn” (ذلك الدين القيم). It directly links divine judgment, worship, and dīn as submission. | terra: "إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ" is immediately joined to the command to worship none but Him, exactly supporting the section's claim that the worshiped one and the Judge are the same.

luna: Jacob says that judgment belongs only to God (إن الحكم إلا لله) as he sends his sons toward Egypt and entrusts them to God; it brings the section's hakim language into the same family peril as 12:80. | terra: Jacob takes precautions yet says "إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ" and trusts Him, distinguishing prudent action from possession of the final decision.

luna: The verse says Joseph could not have taken his brother under the king's dīn (في دين الملك), meaning the king's law or rule; this is a distinct legal sense of the root beside the section's dīn as divine judgment and reckoning. | terra: Joseph could not have taken his brother under "دِينِ الْمَلِكِ" except by God's will; this worldly king's regime displays the source dictionary's dīn sense of governing subjection beside God's final dīn.

luna: The section cites the brother who will remain in Egypt until his father permits him or God judges for him; the verse stages waiting in place for the very “khayru l-ḥākimīn” named in the image. | terra: Joseph's eldest brother refuses to leave until his father permits it or God judges for him, then says He is "خَيْرُ الْحَاكِمِينَ"; judgment is the release from a binding pledge.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to worship God without associating partners, call to Him, and declare that to Him is the return; this supplies the worship-and-return frame for 13:37.
terra: The revelation is sent as an Arabic judgment, and the Prophet is warned not to follow desires after knowledge; revealed حكم restrains appetite through knowledge.
terra: God judges and no one can reverse or review His judgment, then the ayah names Him swift in account; the Judge's decision is both final and answerable to no higher court.

luna: Abraham asks forgiveness for himself, his parents, and believers on “the day the account is established” (يوم يقوم الحساب); this is a prayer oriented toward the reckoning named in the section. | terra: Abraham asks forgiveness for himself, his parents, and believers "يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الْحِسَابُ"; the account itself is pictured as standing or being established.
terra: The curse on Iblis lasts until "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ", making the day of recompense the fixed limit at which deferred judgment arrives.
terra: People swear that God will not raise the dead, and the denial is answered "بَلَىٰ" as a binding true promise; the self-answering logic concerns resurrection directly.
terra: Resurrection will clarify what people disputed and make deniers know their falsehood, adding adjudication to the raising affirmed in 16:38.

luna: The ayah says that everything in heaven and earth belongs to God and that “the dīn is His continually” (وله الدين واصبا); here dīn is devoted submission, a distinct but relevant sense beside the section's Day of Judgment. | terra: All in heaven and earth belongs to God and "لَهُ الدِّينُ وَاصِبًا"; enduring obedience or subjection belongs to the same owner whose judgment governs the final day.
terra: The man ashamed of a daughter deliberates whether to keep her in humiliation or bury her, and "سَاءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ" condemns a judgment that produces the very ظلم judgment should prevent.
terra: God commands justice and beneficence and forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and transgression; divine command performs the corrective prevention from ظلم in the source dictionary.

luna: On the day every soul comes arguing for itself and is fully repaid for its deeds without injustice; this makes the section's dīn as reckoning, judgment, and requital a scene. | terra: Each soul comes arguing for itself, is paid fully for its deeds, and is not wronged; this stages litigants before a judgment that checks injustice.

luna: After people disputed over the Sabbath, the ayah says their Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection; it joins the section's dispute, dīn-day judgment, and return to God. | terra: The Lord will judge on the Day of Resurrection between those who disputed about the Sabbath, joining a concrete legal dispute to final adjudication.

luna: The section's source word ḥikma means wisdom; here the call to God's way is to be made “with wisdom” (بالحكمة), showing wisdom as a means of a sound, corrective address. | terra: Calling to God's way requires wisdom, good instruction, and the best manner of argument; right discernment governs speech meant to correct rather than coerce.

luna: The ayah calls its preceding commands “part of the wisdom” (ذلك مما أوحى إليك ربك من الحكمة) and ends with worship of God alone; it meets the section's wisdom branch and its link between Allah and worship. | terra: The revealed restraints just listed are called part of the Lord's wisdom, and the ayah again forbids setting another deity with God; wisdom orders conduct under the worshiped one.

luna: “Does He who created the heavens and earth not have power to create the like?” is a negative question whose context asserts the Creator's power; it parallels the form and creation-to-resurrection reasoning of the section's cited 75:40. | terra: The deniers are asked whether the Creator of heaven and earth can create their like; the self-answering creation argument leads to an appointed resurrection term.

luna: The passage says God has no partner in His judgment (ولا يشرك في حكمه أحدا); this states the boundary implicit in the section's claim that Allah alone is the wisest Judge. | terra: God admits no one as a partner in His judgment, giving a direct boundary to the section's identification of the worshiped one as sole Judge.
terra: People are presented before their Lord in rows and are told they have come as they were first created, joining origin, return, and appearance for judgment before the record in 18:49.

luna: The record is placed, people fear what it contains, and their Lord wrongs no one; this is a concrete accounting scene for the section's dīn as judgment and reckoning. | terra: The record is set down, deeds are found present, and "لَا يَظْلِمُ رَبُّكَ أَحَدًا"; documentary account displays how the Judge prevents injustice.
terra: Yahya is given "الْحُكْمَ صَبِيًّا"; judgment or wisdom is shown as a divine gift even before ordinary adult experience.
terra: God declares that there is no deity but Him and commands Moses to worship Him, establishing the sole worshiped one before the next ayah announces recompense.
terra: The Hour is coming so every soul may be repaid for what it strives; it completes 20:14's sole worship with the same God's role as final Judge.

luna: Faces are humbled before the Ever-Living Sustainer, and the wrongdoer fails; this joins the section's “standing before al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm” gloss to humility and the boundary against injustice. | terra: Faces are humbled before "الْحَيِّ الْقَيُّومِ" and the bearer of wrongdoing fails, matching the section's scene of creation standing subject before the Living, Self-Sustaining Judge.
terra: Every soul tastes death, is tested by evil and good, and is returned to God; the whole moral trial is bounded by the return to its Judge.
terra: God sets just balances for the Day of Resurrection so no soul is wronged at all, even to a mustard seed; this specifies how the final judgment prevents injustice.
terra: Lot receives "حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا" and is rescued from a town practicing corrupt acts, so discerning judgment is joined to deliverance from wrongdoing.
terra: David and Solomon judge the damaged field while God witnesses their ruling; a concrete dispute makes the meaning of الحكم visible.

terra: God gives Solomon the right understanding of that case and gives both men "حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا"; it closely embodies the source dictionary's wisdom as reaching truth through knowledge and reason.
terra: God will repeat creation as He began it, under a promise binding upon Him; origination guarantees recreation rather than merely suggesting it.

luna: The Prophet prays “My Lord, judge with truth” (رب احكم بالحق); the section's ḥukm as a just decision is here voiced as a plea amid accusations. | terra: The Messenger prays "رَبِّ احْكُمْ بِالْحَقِّ" amid hostile descriptions, making judgment in truth the answer sought under pressure.

luna: This resurrection argument traces human formation through the womb, maturity, and possible return to decrepit age before affirming that God raises the dead; it offers a specific bodily counterpart to the section's movement from best formation toward a low state, though the two passages need not mean the same stage. | terra: Successive human stages and revived earth are displayed to remove doubt about resurrection, making created form evidence for the return before judgment.
terra: The creation stages prove that God is truth, gives life to the dead, and is capable of everything; the inference drawn from 22:5 is made explicit.

luna: The ayah explicitly says the Hour is coming and God will raise those in the graves; it makes the creation sequence in 22:5 bear directly on resurrection, the section's dīn-day question. | terra: The Hour is doubtless and God raises those in the graves, carrying the proof from bodily and earthly formation into the judicial gathering.
terra: God separates the named religious communities on the Day of Resurrection and witnesses everything; the Judge resolves divisions spanning whole communities.
terra: God cancels Satan's intrusion and then "يُحْكِمُ اللَّهُ آيَاتِهِ"; this h-k-m usage visibly performs the source dictionary's restraint for correction and firming.

luna: On that day sovereignty belongs to God, who judges between people; believers who did good are in gardens. The verse joins the section's mastery branch of d-y-n, final ḥukm, and the good outcome of 95:6. | terra: On that Day sovereignty belongs to God and He judges between believers and unbelievers, uniting ownership, the day, and adjudication.

luna: The section calls dīn the day of judgment and cites the root q-w-m behind resurrection; this ayah says God judges between people on the Day of Resurrection over their disagreements. | terra: God will judge on the Day of Resurrection concerning the very matters people disputed, directly identifying the judge's day described in the section.

luna: After describing the stages in the womb, the ayah says God forms the human being as another creation; it supplies a bodily account of the formation called taqwīm in the section. | terra: The embryo passes through measured forms until God produces another creation and is praised as "أَحْسَنُ الْخَالِقِينَ"; excellent formation is the premise for what follows.

luna: The next ayah says that after this formation people will die; it continues the human sequence from 23:14 toward the section's return and final judgment. | terra: After that formation, human beings certainly die; this supplies the transition from first creation to the return discussed by the section.

luna: The next ayah says people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection; it completes 23:14-15 with the return to judgment that follows the section's creation and fall. | terra: After death people are raised on the Day of Resurrection, completing the creator-to-judgment logic of the closing question.

luna: At death, a person pleads “My Lord, send me back” (رب ارجعون) to do good; the section's dictionary form aḥkamtu means “I returned him,” and this scene makes return a denied plea for another chance. | terra: At death a person pleads "رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ" to return and act rightly; the desired return to earthly choice is set against the unavoidable return to judgment.

luna: The next ayah denies the plea in 23:99 and places a barrier until resurrection; it makes the return in the section's dictionary gloss a boundary controlled by God. | terra: The request to return is refused and a barrier remains until resurrection; this boundary distinguishes a revoked earthly return from the final raising no one can evade.
terra: People are asked whether they thought God created them aimlessly and that they would not be returned to Him; creation without return is rejected in a single question.
terra: The response exalts God as the true King and says there is no deity but Him, joining the return of 23:115 to sovereignty and sole worship.
terra: On that day God pays people "دِينَهُمُ الْحَقَّ", their full and true recompense; dīn appears as the just due administered by the Judge.

luna: The section says a party can be called to God's judgment; here people turn away when called to God and the Messenger “to judge between them” (ليحكم بينهم), showing refusal of that call. | terra: When they are called to God and His Messenger "لِيَحْكُمَ بَيْنَهُمْ", a party turns away, exactly staging the summons to judgment described by the section.

luna: Following the refusal in 24:48, this ayah says they come readily if the right is on their side; it identifies self-interest as the boundary that makes their response to judgment unreliable. | terra: When the disputed right favors them, the same refusers come to the Messenger submissively; selective submission exposes desire rather than principled judgment.

luna: The next ayah asks whether their hearts are sick or they doubt, then calls them wrongdoers; it gives the refusal in 24:48 a moral diagnosis rather than treating it as a neutral disagreement. | terra: The passage asks whether they have disease, doubt, or fear that God and His Messenger will be unjust, then identifies them as the wrongdoers; the divine court is explicitly cleared of ظلم.

luna: The section's call to God's judgment is answered here by believers who say “we hear and obey” when called to be judged; it supplies the receptive stance opposite 24:48. | terra: Believers answer the same summons to God's and the Messenger's judgment with "سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا"; judgment and obedient submission meet in the response.
terra: God knows the present state of all, and on the day they are returned to Him He tells them their deeds; exhaustive knowledge grounds the final accounting.
luna: On that day true dominion belongs to the Most Merciful and it is hard for disbelievers; this develops the section's d-y-n branch of mastery and the boundary between outcomes.
terra: Moses says his Lord granted him judgment or wisdom and made him a messenger, identifying حكم as a divinely given capacity after his flight and return.
terra: Abraham hopes his Lord will forgive his fault on "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ"; the Judge's day is approached through personal hope as well as fear.
terra: Abraham asks God to grant him "حُكْمًا" and join him with the righteous, treating sound judgment as a gift that directs a life rightly.

luna: Noah pleads, “judge between me and them decisively” (فافتح بيني وبينهم فتحا) and save him and the believers; like 11:45, this is a distressed prophet entrusting an immediate conflict to God's judgment. | terra: Noah asks God to decide between him and his denying people and save the believers, a non-h-k-m formulation of judgment sought in distress.
terra: The Lord decides Israel's disputes "بِحُكْمِهِ" and is mighty and knowing; judgment here carries the knowledge needed to hit the truth.
terra: At maturity Moses is likewise given "حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا", repeating the union of sound judgment and knowledge behind the section's definition of wisdom.

luna: The ayah says judgment belongs to God and people return to Him (له الحكم وإليه ترجعون), closely joining the section's return and final authority. | terra: The ayah joins "لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ", "لَهُ الْحُكْمُ", and "إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ"; the worshiped one, Judge, and destination of return are explicitly one.

luna: After saying everything perishes except God's face, the ayah says “His is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned” (له الحكم وإليه ترجعون); it joins return and judgment as in the section's reading of 95:5 and 95:8. | terra: After forbidding invocation of another deity, the ayah says everything perishes except God, "لَهُ الْحُكْمُ", and to Him all are returned; it gathers worship, judgment, and return.
terra: Those doing evil imagine they can outrun God and are told "سَاءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ"; their judgment denies the return that divine judgment enforces.
terra: "Does God not know best what is in the breasts of all beings?" uses the same negative-question form to compel acknowledgment of the knowledge required for judgment.
terra: People are asked whether they see how God begins creation and repeats it, and are told that repetition is easy for Him; first creation directly warrants resurrection.
terra: Travel through the earth is commanded to observe how creation began, after which God produces the final creation; reflective knowledge of origins leads to the afterlife.
terra: Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God, making death the unavoidable passage to the return developed by the section.

luna: God originates creation, repeats it, and to Him people return (ثم إليه ترجعون); this is a concise parallel to the section's movement from creation to return. | terra: God begins creation, repeats it, and then people are returned to Him; origination and return are stated as one ordered movement.
terra: God originates creation and then repeats it, which is easiest for Him, and He is the mighty, wise one; recreative power and wisdom belong to the final Judge.

terra: God is named creator, provider, giver of death and life, then the hearers are asked whether any partners do any of this; the question excludes rival objects of worship from the powers leading to return.

luna: Human beings move from weakness to strength and back to weakness and old age; as a human-life sequence, it is a specific reversal beside 95:4-5's best formation and descent, though the section does not identify its “lowest” with old age.
terra: Luqman is given wisdom and told to be grateful; wisdom reaches its right practical conclusion in recognition of the giver.
terra: God makes everything He created good and begins human creation from clay; good formation starts a sequence that ends in return to the Lord.
terra: Human progeny is made from an extract of lowly fluid, adding the bodily stage on which denial of renewed creation will stumble.
terra: God proportions the human, breathes into him, and grants hearing, sight, and hearts; deliberate formation deepens responsibility for the faculties given.
terra: Deniers ask whether, once lost in earth, they can be in a new creation; their real refusal is identified as disbelief in meeting their Lord.
terra: The angel of death takes them fully and then they are returned to their Lord, completing the passage's creation-to-return movement.

luna: The ayah says the Lord will judge between people on the Day of Resurrection over what they differed about; this repeats the section's scene of disputes referred to God's judgment. | terra: The Lord will decide between people on the Day of Resurrection concerning their disputes; the nonlexical "يفصل" repeats judgment as separation.
terra: Once God and His Messenger decide a matter, believing men and women have no remaining choice; divine decision places desire under a binding limit.
terra: Those who deny the Hour are answered "بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّي لَتَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ" by the Knower of the unseen; the yes required by denial is backed by exhaustive divine knowledge.
terra: The Hour comes so that believers may be recompensed for their deeds, supplying the judicial purpose of the emphatic "بَلَىٰ" in 34:3.
terra: The Prophet says the Lord will gather the two sides and decide between them in truth, calling Him the knowing Decider; gathering, knowledge, and just settlement meet in one answer.

terra: Shackles rise to the deniers' chins and force their heads up; this is a Quranic physical analogue to the source dictionary's bridle-piece surrounding the jaw and preventing a creature from rushing free.

luna: At the judgment, no soul is wronged and each is repaid only for what it did; this gives the section's “accounting and requital” gloss of dīn a concrete rule. | terra: On that day no soul is wronged and people receive only what they did; the self-answering resurrection question of 36:81 culminates in exact recompense.
terra: A human created from a drop becomes an open disputant; the created creature's challenge sets up the judgment-bearing question answered in 36:81.
terra: The disputant forgets his own creation and asks who can revive decayed bones, identifying the denial that the following creator argument overturns.
terra: The answer is that the one who originated the bones the first time will revive them and knows every creation; first creation grounds return and divine knowledge.
terra: Within the answer about reviving bones, God brings fire from a green tree; an experienced reversal makes re-creation less remote.

luna: The section cites this negative question about the Creator's ability to make the dead live, answered “Yes” (بلى); like 95:8, the question's form puts the confirming answer in the hearer's mouth. | terra: The negative question asks whether the Creator of heaven and earth can create their like and answers "بَلَىٰ"; creative power places affirmation of resurrection in the listener's mouth.
terra: God's command when He wills a thing is only that it be, and it is; this explains how the creator affirmed in 36:81 effects the return stated in 36:83.
terra: After the creation argument, all dominion is in God's hand and "إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ"; ability to recreate ends in return to the sovereign Judge.

luna: The deniers exclaim, “This is the Day of Judgment” (هذا يوم الدين) when it arrives; it is an exact formulation of the day they are asked not to deny in 95:7. | terra: At resurrection the deniers cry "هَذَا يَوْمُ الدِّينِ"; what was denied becomes a recognized scene before the Judge.

luna: “This is the Day of Decision” (هذا يوم الفصل) is announced to those who denied it; the phrase gives another name to the judgment day glossed in the section as dīn. | terra: Immediately after the cry "This is the Day of dīn," the day is identified as the Day of Decision that they denied; dīn is thus glossed by enacted separation and verdict.
terra: The condemned are stopped because they are to be questioned; physical restraint is exercised for an account, closely realizing the section's primary sense of holding back for judgment.
terra: A speaker asks whether, after death and becoming dust and bones, people will be "لَمَدِينُونَ", brought to account or recompensed; the root is tied directly to resurrection.
terra: "مَا لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ" rebukes the claim that God has daughters; the hearers' verdict is placed under the question of the true Judge.
terra: David is given wisdom and decisive speech, "الْحِكْمَةَ وَفَصْلَ الْخِطَابِ"; wisdom here equips the ruler to separate and settle claims rightly.
terra: Two litigants ask David to judge between them in truth, without exceeding justice, and to guide them to an even path; the parties themselves state the proper work of a judge.
terra: One litigant describes the other's ninety-nine ewes and demand for his single ewe, supplying the concrete imbalance the requested judgment must correct.
terra: David identifies the demand for the single ewe as wrongdoing, then realizes that he has been tested and turns back repentantly; judging another becomes a check upon the judge himself.

luna: David is commanded to judge between people with truth and not follow desire; the section's bridle image of restraint and its definition of ḥukm as preventing injustice meet in this warning. | terra: David is ordered to judge people in truth and not follow desire lest it divert him from God's path; just judgment functions as the rein that checks impulse.
terra: The question rejects treating believers who do right like corrupters or the mindful like the wicked; final judgment must preserve moral distinctions.
luna: The promised reward is identified as “this is what you are promised for the Day of Account” (هذا ما توعدون ليوم الحساب); it states the requital side of the section's dīn gloss.
terra: Iblis's curse is extended to "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ", again marking that day as the terminus of respite and the onset of settled recompense.

luna: The ayah says “to God belongs the pure dīn” (ألا لله الدين الخالص) and contrasts this with worship through intermediaries; this connects the section's mastery/submission branch of d-y-n with its claim that Allah is the one worshiped and the Judge. | terra: Pure dīn belongs to God, false protectors claim to mediate worship, and God judges their dispute; servitude, divine ownership, and adjudication are inseparable.
terra: "أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِكَافٍ عَبْدَهُ" uses the same self-answering negative form to make God's sufficiency for His servant something the hearer must affirm.
terra: "أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِعَزِيزٍ ذِي انْتِقَامٍ" uses the same form to compel acknowledgment of the power that enforces judgment.

luna: The Prophet asks God, Creator of the heavens and earth, to judge between His servants concerning what they differed over; it is another direct plea for the final adjudication named in the section. | terra: The prayer to Creator and Knower asks Him to judge between His servants concerning their disagreements, joining creation, knowledge, and final decision.
luna: After the trumpet is blown a second time, people stand looking (قيام ينظرون); this depicts the rising and standing that the section's qiyāmah gloss connects with the final court.

luna: The record is set, witnesses are brought, and judgment is made “with truth” (وقضي بينهم بالحق) with no one wronged; this stages the just judgment the section names. | terra: The earth shines, the record and witnesses are brought, and people are judged in truth without being wronged; it makes the section's root definition a full courtroom scene.
terra: After the courtroom scene of 39:69, every soul is paid fully for what it did, and God knows their deeds best; the verdict becomes precise recompense.
terra: At Hell's gates the keepers ask whether messengers came, and the condemned answer "بَلَىٰ"; a negative question draws the admission that seals judgment.

luna: Angels glorify their Lord while judgment is made among people with truth; it brings the section's link between the worshiped Allah and the final Judge into one scene. | terra: Angels surround the Throne praising their Lord after judgment is concluded in truth; the courtroom sequence closes by affirming the justice of its Judge.
terra: Those who rejected God alone but believed when partners were joined are told "فَالْحُكْمُ لِلَّهِ"; exclusive judgment answers a failure of exclusive worship.

luna: On the day people appear with nothing hidden, the question “whose is the kingdom today?” is answered “God's, the One, the Prevailing”; it develops the section's d-y-n branch of mastery and subjection. | terra: When all are exposed, the question "Whose is the kingdom today?" is answered: God's, the One, the Subduer; ownership and universal subjection frame the recompense of the next ayah.

luna: “Today every soul is repaid for what it earned; no injustice today” (اليوم تجزى كل نفس بما كسبت لا ظلم اليوم) unpacks the section's dīn as accounting and requital, while echoing ḥukm's restraint from injustice. | terra: "الْيَوْمَ تُجْزَىٰ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ" is followed by "لَا ظُلْمَ الْيَوْمَ"; the Judge's day is precisely a restraint of wrongdoing.

luna: God “judges with truth” (يقضي بالحق), while those invoked besides Him cannot judge anything; the contrast gives force to the section's identification of Allah as al-ḥākim. | terra: God decides in truth, while the beings invoked besides Him cannot decide anything; sole worship and sole effective judgment are distinguished from powerless rivals.
luna: Moses seeks refuge in his Lord from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Account; it gives the section's dīn-day judgment a concrete posture of fearing God's verdict.
terra: During the inhabitants of the Fire's dispute, the arrogant say that God has already judged between the servants; the verdict has become an irreversible condition shared by both parties.
terra: Hell's keepers ask "أَوَلَمْ تَكُ تَأْتِيكُمْ رُسُلُكُمْ" and the sufferers answer "بَلَىٰ"; the forced yes acknowledges the evidence behind the sentence.

luna: God promises support to messengers and believers “on the day the witnesses stand” (يوم يقوم الأشهاد); the standing witnesses evoke the section's qiyāmah as a day of standing before judgment. | terra: God promises to aid His messengers and believers "يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الْأَشْهَادُ"; witnesses standing turns the final judgment into a courtroom event.
terra: God makes the earth and sky, forms people and makes their forms good, provides for them, and is proclaimed Lord; excellent formation grounds the worship commanded at the ayah's close.
terra: The Living one, with no deity besides Him, is to be called upon with dīn made sincere; the worshiped Living Lord is the one before whom the section pictures creation standing.
terra: With collars on their necks and chains, the condemned are dragged away; it extends the source dictionary's physical restraint image from a guiding bridle to punitive restraint.
terra: When God's command comes, the matter is decided in truth and falsifiers lose; the arrival of judgment turns contested claims into a settled outcome.
terra: The speaking skins say that God created people the first time and that they are returned to Him; first formation and bodily testimony converge at the return.

luna: The section glosses calling someone to God's ruling; here whatever people dispute “its judgment belongs to God” (فحكمه إلى الله), directly naming that recourse. | terra: Every disputed matter has its judgment with God; the speaker then names Him as Lord, trusts Him, and turns to Him, binding adjudication to return and servitude.
terra: God sends the Book in truth and the balance, then warns that the Hour may be near; measured justice and final judgment are placed side by side.

luna: Jesus says he has brought wisdom (بالحكمة) and come to clarify some matters over which people differ; this joins the section's wisdom branch to its account of judgment settling dispute. | terra: Jesus comes with wisdom and says he will clarify some disputed matters, linking wisdom to the accurate resolution of disagreement.

luna: The ayah calls the appointed gathering “the Day of Decision” (يوم الفصل); it is a further direct formulation of dīn as the day of judgment. | terra: The Day of Decision is the appointed time for everyone, another direct formulation of the final settlement's universality.

luna: After the Children of Israel differed despite receiving knowledge, their Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection; this is a concrete instance of the section's promised settling of disagreements. | terra: People differ after knowledge through rivalry, and the Lord judges their disputes on the Resurrection Day; final judgment corrects knowledge distorted by desire.
terra: The Prophet is placed upon a divinely ordered way and told not to follow the desires of those who do not know; knowledge and law act as a rein on appetite.
terra: Wrongdoers suppose they will be made equal to believers in life and death, and the ayah says "سَاءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ"; bad human judgment is exposed by the just distinction of the next ayah.

luna: The ayah says each soul is repaid for what it earned and no one is wronged; its pairing of recompense and justice makes explicit the relation between dīn and the section's anti-injustice definition of ḥukm. | terra: God created heaven and earth in truth so each soul may be recompensed for what it earned without injustice; creation is ordered toward the just settlement implied by 95:8.
terra: God gives life, causes death, and gathers everyone on the doubtless Day of Resurrection; creation and death issue in the judicial gathering.
luna: Every community is seen kneeling and called to its record; this gives the section's judgment-day image a collective scene and a bodily posture distinct from standing before the Lord.
terra: Each person has ranks according to deeds so God may pay them fully without injustice; differentiated recompense embodies accurate judgment.

luna: A negative question about the Creator's power to revive the dead is answered “Yes indeed” (بلى إنه على كل شيء قدير); this is another explicit resurrection form of the section's rhetorical question. | terra: A negative question asks whether the God who created the heavens and earth can revive the dead, then answers "بَلَىٰ"; it is a direct parallel to both 36:81 and 75:40.
terra: At the Fire the same question "أَلَيْسَ هَذَا بِالْحَقِّ" draws "بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّنَا", showing the forced affirmation that follows earlier denial.
terra: A transgressing party is resisted until it returns to God's command, after which reconciliation must be just; return, restraint, reform, and equity form one process.
terra: God asks whether first creation wearied Him and identifies the real problem as doubt about a new creation; the rhetorical question makes origination evidence for return.

luna: The section cites the oath's answer “the dīn will surely occur” (وإن الدين لواقع); it asserts the certainty of the reckoning named in 95:7. | terra: "وَإِنَّ الدِّينَ لَوَاقِعٌ" asserts under oath that the reckoning or recompense must occur, answering the denial asked about in 95:7.
terra: The hearers are asked whether they were created from nothing or are themselves the creators; the rhetorical alternatives compel admission of a creator.
terra: They are next asked whether they created heaven and earth, with their lack of certainty exposed; the broadened creation question reinforces the premise behind resurrection and judgment.
terra: God owns heaven and earth so that evil is recompensed by deeds and excellence rewarded with the best; ownership serves discriminating judgment.
terra: Human striving will be repaid with the fullest recompense, describing dīn as exact payment rather than a vague consequence.
terra: The final destination is to the Lord, joining the full recompense of 53:41 to return.
terra: God causes both death and life, giving the agent of return sovereign command over both thresholds.
terra: God creates the male and female pair, beginning a formation sequence parallel to the one behind 75:40.
terra: The pair comes from an emitted drop, supplying the first bodily origin in that sequence.
terra: The other creation is incumbent upon God, turning first formation into an explicit promise of recreation.

luna: The section's dictionary branch defines ḥikma as right insight by knowledge and reason; this ayah names a far-reaching wisdom (حكمة بالغة) but says warnings do not benefit, showing wisdom's presence against refusal to heed. | terra: The warnings are described as consummate wisdom, though warnings do not benefit the refusers; wisdom reaches the truth while leaving hearers responsible for refusal.
terra: "Is the recompense of excellence anything but excellence?" is a self-answering question that makes fitting repayment appear undeniable.
terra: The deniers' scalding hospitality is identified as their reception on "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ", giving concrete consequence to the day denied in 95:7.
terra: "We created you; why then do you not affirm?" opens a chain of questions turning bodily origin into a demanded confession.
terra: The hearer is directed to the fluid emitted in generation, supplying the concrete beginning of the creator argument.
terra: The question asks whether humans create that life or God does, forcing recognition of the creator before death and recreation are discussed.
terra: God says that He has decreed death among people and cannot be outstripped, making death a measured divine appointment.
terra: God can replace people with their likes and produce them in a form they do not know; transformation and renewed creation defeat human control.
terra: Knowledge of the first creation is invoked as the reason people should remember, completing the passage's inference from origin to recreation.
terra: The soul reaches the throat while those present watch; this bedside scene makes the challenge about being unsubjected and returning it in 56:86-87 concrete.

luna: The section's d-y-n branch includes mastering or subjugating someone; this challenge asks why, if people are not under God's power or recompense, they cannot return the departing soul (ترجعونها). | terra: At a dying person's bedside the challengers are asked whether they are "غَيْرَ مَدِينِينَ", outside subjection or recompense; the source dictionary's dīn sense of being under mastery becomes existential.
terra: They are challenged to return the departing soul if truthful; failure to turn it back proves the subjection named in 56:86 and points toward God's final return.
terra: Hypocrites ask believers "أَلَمْ نَكُنْ مَعَكُمْ" and receive "بَلَىٰ", but a barrier now separates them; verbal affirmation cannot erase the earlier choices under judgment.
terra: Messengers, scripture, and the balance are sent so people may uphold justice; revealed order equips humanity to perform the corrective purpose ascribed to judgment.

luna: This ayah says family ties and children will not avail on the Day of Resurrection and that God will decide between people; it recalls Noah's appeal for his son while placing kinship under final judgment.
terra: Rules governing believing migrant women are called "حُكْمُ اللَّهِ يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ", showing divine judgment ordering a difficult human separation.
terra: The death people flee will meet them, then they are "تُرَدُّونَ" to the Knower who reports their deeds; unavoidable death becomes the road back to judgment.
luna: God fashions people and makes their forms beautiful, “then to Him is the destination” (وإليه المصير); this joins the best formation of 95:4 to the return in 95:5.

terra: Deniers claim they will not be raised, and the Prophet is commanded to answer "بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّي" before saying they will be told their deeds; affirmation, resurrection, and account are explicit.
luna: The day God gathers people is called the Day of Loss and Gain, when faith and deeds lead to forgiveness and a garden; it gives dīn's reckoning and return a concrete division of outcomes.
terra: Each cast group is asked by Hell's keepers "أَلَمْ يَأْتِكُمْ نَذِيرٌ"; the negative question prepares the explicit affirmation in the next ayah.
terra: The group answers "بَلَىٰ قَدْ جَاءَنَا نَذِيرٌ" and admits denial; the section's grammar becomes a confession at judgment.
terra: The question whether the submitting are to be treated like criminals rejects an indiscriminate outcome, clarifying that just judgment must distinguish morally unlike lives.
terra: "مَا لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ" challenges the hearers' warped verdict, a direct foil to the closing affirmation of God as best Judge.
terra: The faithful are those who affirm "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ"; their certainty is the direct counterpart to the denial challenged in 95:7.

luna: The damned say they used to deny the Day of Requital (نكذب بيوم الدين); it shows what the section's question asks its hearer to face. | terra: The condemned confess "وَكُنَّا نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ", showing the final consequence of the denial questioned by the surah.
terra: The human is asked whether he thinks God will not assemble his bones, making bodily resurrection the denied claim under examination.
terra: "بَلَىٰ" answers the bone question and says God can restore even the fingertips; exact recreation supplies another Quranic model of affirmative response to denial.
terra: "إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ الْمَسَاقُ" makes the dying person's drive end at the Lord, linking the same surah's creation argument to final return.

luna: “Does man think he will be left neglected?” (أيحسب الإنسان أن يترك سدى) precedes the creation stages and resurrection question in the same surah; it makes explicit the section's implication that the human is not left without final judgment. | terra: Before recounting human formation, the surah asks whether the human thinks he will be left without purpose or obligation; creation is thereby directed toward accountability.

luna: The section points to the stages listed in Sūrat al-Qiyāmah; this preceding ayah begins that sequence with a drop of emitted fluid, before 75:38 says He created and proportioned. | terra: The human being was first a drop of emitted fluid; this is the opening bodily stage in the argument that creation entails the power to resurrect and judge.

luna: This is the section's cited “He created and proportioned” (فخلق فسوى), a direct parallel to human creation in the best taqwīm in 95:4. | terra: "فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ" supplies the creating and proportioning premise which the section says leads to the final question about reviving the dead.

luna: The next ayah says God made from the human being the two kinds, male and female; it continues the human-creation sequence around the section's cited 75:38. | terra: God makes the created human into the two sexes, completing the sequence between "فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ" and the final self-answering resurrection question.

luna: The section explicitly compares the final question of Sūrat al-Qiyāmah: “Is not that One able to give life to the dead?” (أليس ذلك بقادر على أن يحيي الموتى). Its negative question expects assent to resurrection, as does 95:8's question expecting assent to God's judgment. | terra: "أَلَيْسَ ذَٰلِكَ بِقَادِرٍ" matches 95:8's form exactly: a negative question makes the hearer affirm that the creator can resurrect.

luna: The ayah calls the judgment day “the Day of Decision” (ليوم الفصل); it names the day by the separation and ruling that the section associates with dīn. | terra: The delayed parties are appointed for the Day of Decision, a repeated Quranic name for the section's day of judgment.

luna: The next ayah repeats the question “what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?”; it intensifies the day-name in 77:13 before the surah describes it. | terra: "What will make you know what the Day of Decision is?" closely repeats Infitar's question about what makes one know the Day of dīn.

luna: The ayah calls it the Day of Decision and says people are gathered with earlier peoples; it makes the judgment-day name in 77:13 concrete as a gathered court. | terra: The Day of Decision gathers the present deniers and earlier peoples, turning the name into a universal courtroom assembly.

luna: “The Day of Decision has an appointed time” (إن يوم الفصل كان ميقاتا); this states the certainty and appointment of the judgment day that the section calls dīn. | terra: The Day of Decision is a fixed appointment, expressing the certainty and measured timing of the Judge's day.
luna: The transgressors are described as not expecting an account (لا يرجون حسابا); this directly echoes the section's gloss of dīn as ḥisāb and its challenge to denial.

luna: On the day the Spirit and angels stand in rows before the Most Merciful, no one speaks without permission; it gives bodily form to the qiyāmah scene in the section's q-w-m gloss. | terra: The Spirit and angels stand in rows on the final day and speak only by the Merciful's permission, extending the section's image of creation standing before its Lord.
luna: The ayah calls the day “the True Day” and says whoever wills may take a return to his Lord; it joins the section's final judgment and return motifs.

luna: The section's bridle image is restraint that corrects; here the one who fears standing before the Lord restrains the self from desire (ونهى النفس عن الهوى), an inward counterpart to that restraint. | terra: The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire receives the Garden; it unites the courtroom stance with the source dictionary's restraint.
luna: The next ayah names Paradise as the abode of the person who restrained the self in 79:40; it supplies the outcome of restraint before judgment.
luna: The human is created from a drop and proportioned (فقدره); this is a close formulation of the section's 95:4 image of the human made in best proportion.
luna: After creation and proportioning in 80:19, this ayah says God made the way easy; it continues the sequence of what the Creator does for the human.
luna: The human is then made to die and buried; this marks the low point between the fashioned human of the section and return to judgment.
luna: The next ayah says that when God wills, He raises the human; after death in 80:21 this makes return from the grave part of the creation sequence.
luna: God creates, fashions, and proportionally forms the human being (خلقك فسواك فعدلك); this closely parallels 95:4's creation in the best taqwīm.
luna: The next ayah says God composed the human being in whatever form He willed; it specifies the fashioned form in 82:7 and makes a direct parallel to 95:4's taqwīm.
luna: This ayah says people “deny the Day of dīn” (تكذبون بالدين), the precise denial questioned in 95:7.
luna: After 82:9 names denial of the Day of dīn, this ayah introduces the appointed recorders; it shows that the denied day involves deeds being kept.
luna: The next ayah describes those recorders as honorable scribes, specifying the accounting scene introduced after the denial in 82:9.
luna: The final neighbor says the recorders know what people do; it makes the record in 82:10-11 relevant to the section's dīn as account.
terra: The wicked enter the blaze on "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ"; the named day carries enacted recompense, not an abstract calendar label.

luna: The section cites this question, “what will make you know what the Day of dīn is?” (وما أدراك ما يوم الدين); it opens the same reckoning day that 95:7 asks people not to deny. | terra: "وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا يَوْمُ الدِّينِ" is the section's quoted question naming the Judge's day of reckoning and recompense.

luna: This ayah repeats the question from 82:17; the repetition sustains the question before 82:19 answers that command on that day belongs to God. | terra: The repeated question about "يَوْمُ الدِّينِ" intensifies the inability to master that day's meaning before the following ayah supplies its decisive feature.

luna: The section cites this answer: on that day no soul controls anything for another, and command belongs to God (والأمر يومئذ لله); it clarifies the sovereignty in “Master of the Day of dīn.” | terra: No soul can do anything for another on that day and "الْأَمْرُ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلَّهِ"; this is the section's answer that all command then belongs to the Judge.
terra: "Do they not think that they will be raised?" is a negative question exposing the premise behind fraudulent measure and preparing the standing scene of 83:6.
terra: The raising just asked about is "for a tremendous day," supplying the temporal bridge to humanity's standing before the Lord in 83:6.

luna: The section's dictionary description of qiyāmah says creatures stand before the Living, Sustaining One; this ayah says people stand before the Lord of the worlds (لرب العالمين). | terra: "يَوْمَ يَقُومُ النَّاسُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ" is the exact standing-before-the-Lord scene used by the section to explain qiyāmah from the q-w-m root.

luna: This ayah identifies those who deny the Day of dīn (يكذبون بيوم الدين), a direct parallel to the challenge in 95:7. | terra: The transgressing deniers are identified as those who deny "يَوْمِ الدِّينِ", a direct repetition of the section's link between denial and final judgment.
terra: "إِنَّ إِلَيْنَا إِيَابَهُمْ" makes the people's homeward return belong to God alone, beginning a compact end-of-surah counterpart to Tīn's close.
terra: "ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا حِسَابَهُمْ" makes their account God's charge, completing 88:25's return with the Judge's reckoning.
terra: "إِنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الرُّجْعَىٰ" places return to the Lord directly against the human transgression born of imagining oneself self-sufficient.
terra: "Does he not know that God sees?" uses a negative question to force acknowledgment of the knowledge that makes transgression accountable.
luna: People are commanded to worship God sincerely, making the dīn purely His; this uses dīn as submission or worship, the secondary sense that helps explain the section's d-y-n and ilāh connection.
luna: People emerge in separate groups to see their deeds; this is a compact scene of the reckoning that the section calls dīn.
luna: The section connects dīn with account and requital; here even an atom's weight of good is seen, giving a smallest measure to the judgment of deeds.
luna: The matching statement that even an atom's weight of evil is seen supplies the other side of the reckoning and balances 99:7.
luna: The image of weighed deeds makes judgment measurable: those whose scales are heavy reach a pleasing life, giving a concrete form to the section's accounting and requital.
luna: This next ayah names the pleasing life of those with heavy scales in 101:6; it adds the reward side to the weighed judgment.
luna: The matching case of light scales states the adverse boundary of the weighing in 101:6, a concrete reversal of favorable requital.
luna: The next ayah calls the light-weigher's destination “Hāwiyah”; it specifies the adverse outcome of judgment in 101:8.
luna: This question introduces the explanation of Hāwiyah after the light scales in 101:8-9; the judgment's destination is made explicit in its neighbor.
luna: The answer names it a “blazing fire” (نار حامية), completing 101:10's account of the light-weigher's outcome.
luna: The section reads 95:4-6 as human formation followed by a fall with believers excepted; “the human is in loss” (إن الإنسان لفي خسر) gives a close reversal of that elevated human image.

luna: The exception of those who believe and do right, urge truth, and urge patience mirrors 95:6's exception of believers who do good from the lowly outcome; the two short surahs share a human-loss/faithful-exception pattern.

luna: The surah opens by asking about one who denies al-dīn; the following treatment of pushing aside the orphan makes denial of requital visible in conduct. | terra: "أَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي يُكَذِّبُ بِالدِّينِ" directly parallels 95:7's question about denying the reckoning and lets the following conduct expose what that denial means.
luna: The next ayah depicts the denier from 107:1 as one who repulses the orphan; it gives a concrete social consequence to denying the day of judgment.
luna: The continuation condemns failure to urge feeding the poor; beside the denial in 107:1, it shows conduct that the section's final Judge will weigh.

luna: “For you is your dīn and for me mine” uses dīn for a way of worship, not the Day of Judgment meant in 95:7; that difference matters because the section also develops d-y-n as subjection and links Allah to worship.
